routes.description: Establish that objective moral values require a transcendent standard of goodness and that objective duties require authoritative imperatives, then show that a necessarily good divine nature and commands grounded in that nature provide those foundations while naturalism does not.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it connects objective value to God's necessarily good nature, objective duty to competent divine authority, and the inadequacy of evolutionary, cultural, preference-based, or well-being facts to supply equivalent objective and binding foundations.

motionBridge.description: Show that objective moral values and duties have a supernatural rather than wholly natural ontological foundation.

centralBridges.description: Explain how God's necessarily good nature constitutes a nonarbitrary standard of objective moral value.
Explain how commands issued by competent divine authority and constrained by divine goodness constitute objective moral duties.
Show why natural facts about evolution, consciousness, preference, suffering, or flourishing do not alone establish objective moral value or binding obligation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish the existence and ground of moral facts from moral language, moral knowledge, and disagreement about their application.
Account for the agency and responsibility presupposed by objective duties and address whether naturalistic determinism can sustain them.

routes.description: Establish that value arises through conscious experience, that facts about suffering and flourishing permit objective comparison and correction, and that rational scientific inquiry can investigate those facts, while showing that divine nature, commands, or revelation are unnecessary or unsuitable foundations.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it derives an objective natural standard from conscious well-being, explains how inquiry can distinguish better and worse states independently of current opinion, and shows that supernatural authority neither supplies a necessary standard nor resolves arbitrariness and harmful-command objections.

motionBridge.description: Show that objective moral values and duties can be founded in natural facts about conscious creatures without supernatural authority.

centralBridges.description: Establish conscious experience as the domain in which suffering, flourishing, and morally relevant value can exist.
Explain how movement away from extreme misery toward flourishing supports objective comparisons and allows preferences, practices, and judgments to be mistaken.
Show how objective reasoning and scientific inquiry can investigate natural facts governing conscious well-being despite foundational axioms and first-person experience.
Show why defining divine nature as good or grounding duties in commands does not independently establish goodness and can conflict with judgments about suffering and harm.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend well-being as a usable objective standard despite incomplete definitions, plural forms of flourishing, and difficult boundary cases.
Address whether competing revelations, inherited traditions, and disputed purported commands provide reliable access to moral truth.

sections.title: The Ontological Ground of Objective Moral Value
sections.rationale: This issue tests the primary competing foundations: necessarily good divine nature on the supernatural route and conscious experience, suffering, and flourishing on the natural route.

sections.title: Well-Being, Moral Objectivity, and Scientific Inquiry
sections.rationale: This issue covers whether natural facts permit objective comparisons, correction of preferences and cultures, and rational investigation despite axioms, subjective experience, or imprecise boundaries.

sections.title: From Facts to Objective Duties and Responsibility
sections.rationale: This issue addresses how either route moves from descriptions or values to binding obligations, including authority, the fact-value distinction, agency, ability, and responsibility.

sections.title: Divine Goodness, Command, and Nonarbitrariness
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether divine nature constrains commands nonarbitrarily and whether commands involving apparent harm can be assessed by a standard independent of their asserted source.

sections.title: Moral Ontology, Knowledge, Disagreement, and Revelation
sections.rationale: This issue distinguishes moral reality from access to it and tests the significance of disagreement, competing religious traditions, inherited belief, and shared inquiry for each foundational route.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Objective moral values and duties are independent of human opinion and require a sound foundation that theism supplies but atheism does not.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly introduces Craig, and the uninterrupted opening address begins immediately after the timing cue.

response.rationale: This constructive move states the two conditional contentions that organize the supernatural-foundation route; it has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly establishes the principal burden and the conditional scope of the case.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is readily recoverable, and the explicit qualification that the claims are conditional keeps its scope stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conditional framing is careful, but the necessity of a theistic foundation is announced before its decisive warrants are supplied.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The two conditional contentions form a coherent route, though this span does not yet supply the bridges that establish them.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move clearly states its thesis but, as an opening roadmap, provides little supporting evidence or rival comparison within this span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly states the completion condition for the supernatural-foundation motion bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: This opening thesis primarily declares Craig's own case and does not yet depend on construing a developed opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig explicitly presents two conditional contentions: theism supplies a sound foundation and atheism does not.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: God's necessarily holy and loving nature grounds objective moral values, while divine commands consistent with that nature constitute objective moral duties.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Craig's explicitly announced opening speech and develops his labeled first contention in a continuous first-person presentation.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the central value-and-duty architecture of Craig's route and has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly articulates both the divine-nature standard and command-based account of obligation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The value and duty claims are distinct and recoverable, although the relevant account of necessity and competent authority remains compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The account offers a coherent necessary constraint on commands, but it asserts grounding without fully defending the constitutive relation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Separating values grounded in divine nature from duties constituted by commands is coherent, with one material constitutive bridge compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The holy-and-loving constraint addresses arbitrariness, but the move does not independently establish why nature and commands have the claimed authority.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable divine-nature bridge and also materially bears on the commands bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The span chiefly develops Craig's positive account rather than relying on a contestable representation of an opposing position.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig states that values exist independently of humans and that duties are constituted by commands consistent with God's holy and loving nature.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: On atheistic naturalism, evolved human moral beliefs and concern for human welfare are adaptive products without an objective basis that privileges them over other biological dispositions.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig expressly turns to his second contention, and the same uninterrupted opening speech continues through the naturalistic and evolutionary argument.

response.rationale: This constructive move advances the naturalism-grounding deficit and has no earlier opposing locked target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it squarely raises the missing objective-status bridge for evolved moral dispositions.

precisionFindings.rationale: The grounding challenge is recoverable, but the move shifts broadly among atheism, naturalism, evolutionary origin, worth, and objectivity.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Evolutionary origins can create a debunking or grounding challenge, but they do not by themselves establish that no natural objective basis exists.

charity.alternative: A naturalist may distinguish the evolutionary origin of moral beliefs from the truth-makers or reasons that make some beliefs correct.
charity.decisiveQualification: An evolutionary genealogy alone does not eliminate every natural realist or reasons-based account.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from accidental evolutionary origin to absence of objective worth or truth leaves a substantial genealogy-to-ontology bridge unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The span relies mainly on broad assertions about accidental biological status rather than representative evidence or comparison with naturalist rivals.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central claim that evolutionary and biological facts do not alone ground objective value.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument presses a legitimate explanatory challenge but substantially compresses the strongest naturalist distinction between belief formation and moral truth.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig characterizes humans as accidental natural products and asks what objective basis could privilege human worth or evolved concern.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Defining moral goodness as conscious-creature well-being makes the claim that maximizing well-being is good tautological and does not explain why well-being is objectively morally valuable.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig names Harris and his proposed solution directly while continuing the same clearly attributed opening address without a speaker transition.

response.rationale: Although chronologically constructive in the locked topology, the move attacks the well-being standard by alleging a definitional tautology.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it identifies a specific explanatory deficit in equating moral goodness with conscious-creature well-being.

precisionFindings.rationale: The circularity challenge is clear, though it implicitly assumes Harris offers a strict reductive definition rather than a substantive identification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The tautology follows under a strict definition, but the conclusion overstates matters unless alternative identity or grounding readings are excluded.

charity.alternative: Harris's claim may be a substantive identification or proposed naturalistic criterion rather than a merely verbal redefinition.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even on that reading, an argument is still needed for why well-being exhausts moral value.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The critique coherently exposes that a definition cannot alone provide an independent moral warrant, though it may misclassify the proposed identity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It is supported by Harris's reported formulation but does not compare the stronger substantive-identity interpretation in sufficient depth.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central objective-well-being bridge by challenging the standard's noncircular justification.

representationalCharity.rationale: Craig captures the remaining explanatory demand but frames the opposing position too quickly as a semantic trick.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig quotes the definition of good as supporting conscious-creature well-being and argues that the resulting maximization claim becomes tautological.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Natural science describes facts but cannot generate objective obligations, which require authoritative moral imperatives rather than evolutionary advantage, taboo, or social conditioning.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig introduces a distinct second question about duties and sustains the argument in the same uninterrupted opening speech.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies Craig's central authority-based account of obligation and has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly identifies the fact-to-duty gap and proposes authoritative imperatives as the missing element.

precisionFindings.rationale: The fact-versus-obligation contrast is clear, but claims about science, naturalism, and animals are stated with overly broad scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The is-to-ought challenge is substantial, but the necessity of divine authority is not established merely by excluding bare description.

charity.alternative: Naturalist theories may ground reasons or obligations in natural facts plus rational, contractual, or constitutive principles rather than bare scientific descriptions.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such theories still owe an account of the normatively authoritative bridge from those facts and principles.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The descriptive-to-normative gap is coherent, but the further inference that authoritative divine imperatives are required remains materially underargued.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move provides conceptual examples but no sustained comparison showing that alternative naturalistic accounts cannot supply binding reasons.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable divine-command bridge by arguing that objective duty requires authoritative imperatives.

representationalCharity.rationale: Craig states the legitimate bridge demand but narrows the naturalist alternatives too sharply to animals, conditioning, or description alone.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig contrasts scientific descriptions with obligations and argues that flourishing facts, evolutionary advantage, and social conditioning do not themselves command action.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: If human actions are causally determined without relevant freedom or control, the responsibility presupposed by objective moral duty is unavailable.
moves.attributionBasis: The same speaker labels this as a second problem and explicitly attributes the determinist position and its implications to Harris.

response.rationale: This constructive move advances the subsidiary agency-responsibility bridge and has no earlier opposing locked target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it squarely states the challenge that responsibility requires relevant freedom or control.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is recoverable, but the move does not specify the kind or degree of control required for responsibility.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Rejecting libertarian and compatibilist freedom creates a serious challenge, but the categorical conclusion needs a defended responsibility principle.

charity.alternative: A determinist may revise desert responsibility while retaining prospective responsibility, answerability, or social practices grounded in agency capacities.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those revised notions may not supply the objective desert responsibility Craig's duty account presupposes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional is plausible under a control requirement, but that requirement and the rejection of every responsibility-compatible alternative remain unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The cited rejection and quoted characterization provide some support, while the universal claim about responsibility exceeds the documented premises.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary bridge concerning agency, control, and responsibility under naturalistic determinism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies a genuine tension but treats all morally relevant responsibility as eliminated without addressing revisionary alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig attributes rejection of libertarian and compatibilist freedom to Harris and infers that objective moral responsibility is therefore unavailable.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Conscious experience is a necessary condition for value because changes in the universe can matter only if they can affect a conscious system.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris explicitly announces his reduction of value to conscious-creature well-being and then develops the consciousness component in his own continuous speech.

response.rationale: This constructive move establishes consciousness as the proposed domain of value and has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, the rock-universe contrast directly motivates the necessary-consciousness condition.

precisionFindings.rationale: The necessary-condition claim is clear and stable, with an implicit restriction to morally or experientially relevant value.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The thought experiment fits the limited claim that value requires at least possible significance for conscious experience.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from a consciousness-free universe lacking happiness, suffering, good, or evil to a necessary condition is clear, with one bounded implicit scope bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The thought experiment is apt conceptual support, though it does not compare possible nonexperiential theories of value.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable central bridge locating morally relevant value in conscious experience.

representationalCharity.rationale: The span principally offers Harris's own necessary-condition argument and does not rely on weakening a developed opposing view.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris contrasts a universe of rocks with one containing conscious systems and argues that changes matter only where consciousness can be affected.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: The worst possible misery for every conscious creature is bad, supplying a minimal objective standard from which better states and factual mistakes about moral progress follow.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris explicitly turns from consciousness to well-being and carries the worst-misery thought experiment through the final delivered row of this argumentative move.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the minimal objective anchor for Harris's well-being route and has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it presents a clear limiting case intended to ground objective better-and-worse comparisons.

precisionFindings.rationale: The worst-possible-misery case and its role as a minimal starting assumption are explicit and readily recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The badness judgment is strongly intuitive, but further premises are required to derive a complete objective moral standard or duties.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The limiting case establishes at least one plausible evaluative anchor, but the bridge from that anchor to general moral progress remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The universal-misery thought experiment is powerful conceptual support, though it does not establish the full structure or content of morality.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central objective-well-being bridge through an explicit better-and-worse baseline.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents a positive limiting-case argument without materially construing an opposing theory.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris asks the audience to imagine maximal suffering for every conscious creature and identifies that condition as objectively bad.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Because moral questions concern conscious experience, minds are natural phenomena, and natural facts govern well-being, moral truth can be investigated scientifically.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted first-person presentation occurs within Harris's speech and develops his characteristic moral-landscape account.

response.rationale: This constructive move connects mind-dependent moral questions to natural facts and scientific investigation; it has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly supplies the natural-phenomena and factual-investigation steps of the inquiry route.

precisionFindings.rationale: The route is recoverable, though 'science' ranges between empirical investigation and rational inquiry more generally.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Natural dependence supports empirical inquiry, but it does not by itself show that science determines every evaluative or normative premise.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The mind-to-nature-to-science chain is coherent, but the transition from facts influencing well-being to moral truth leaves a material normative bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The dependence of minds on nature supplies support, while the broader jurisdictional conclusion about moral truth is insufficiently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central rational-inquiry bridge by making well-being a subject of natural investigation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops Harris's affirmative research program rather than depending on a detailed opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris argues that good and evil depend on minds, minds are natural phenomena, and natural facts influence conscious well-being.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Conduct and preferences can be objectively mistaken when they reliably frustrate creaturely well-being, independently of whether individuals or cultures presently endorse them.
moves.attributionBasis: The continuous remarks remain in Harris's speech, with explicit first-person examples and a direct reference to Craig's contrary position.

components.text: Explain why evolved or culturally endorsed preferences can nevertheless be objectively mistaken rather than merely different.
Explain how objective error about conduct yields genuinely binding obligation rather than only an evaluative comparison.

response.rationale: The move directly answers the relativizing challenge by tying error to reliable frustration of well-being, but it does not fully answer the separate authority-to-duty demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive objective-error component while leaving the binding-obligation component unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objective-error claim is clear, with an implicit assumption that relevant well-being effects are sufficiently identifiable and comparable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Reliable frustration can support objective criticism conditional on the standard, but the move does not independently establish the standard's authority.

charity.alternative: Craig's objection is not merely that values differ, but that natural well-being facts lack an objective moral or obligatory status.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing instrumental failure relative to well-being answers relativism more directly than it answers the grounding of moral authority.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Given well-being as a standard, conduct can coherently be objectively defective by reliably defeating that standard; the grounding premise remains assumed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move offers concrete kinds of mistaken preference, but the excerpt provides limited representative support and little alternative comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally attacks the claim that natural preferences and welfare facts cannot support objective moral correction.

representationalCharity.rationale: Harris addresses the strongest relativism component fairly but partially assimilates the deeper ontological and duty objection to simple parity among preferences.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris rejects parity among all values and argues that preferences can be objectively wrong when they predictably undermine personal or shared well-being.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Science itself depends on values such as evidence, logical consistency, understanding, and intellectual honesty, so a categorical fact-value divide cannot exclude morality from rational inquiry.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted conclusion of Harris's speech presents a first-person scientific example before the applause and moderator transition.

response.rationale: This constructive move supports the rational-inquiry bridge and has no earlier opposing locked target under the immutable topology.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it gives a concrete analogy showing that inquiry already relies on nonoptional epistemic norms.

precisionFindings.rationale: The argument is recoverable, though 'values' may conflate epistemic standards, aims of inquiry, and moral values.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Science presupposes epistemic norms, but this does not alone erase every distinction between empirical facts and moral conclusions.

charity.alternative: A critic can accept epistemic norms within science while maintaining that moral norms require a distinct justificatory bridge.
charity.decisiveQualification: The analogy weakens a categorical value-free picture of inquiry without proving that moral values have the same status as epistemic norms.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The example coherently rebuts a wholly value-free conception of inquiry, while the inference to moral science contains a material analogy bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The chemistry example is specific and relevant, though it does not compare theories distinguishing epistemic justification from moral grounding.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central rational-inquiry bridge by identifying epistemic standards internal to scientific practice.

representationalCharity.rationale: Harris fairly exposes dependence on epistemic standards but presses the analogy beyond what its strongest qualified form establishes.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris uses disagreement over water's composition to show that scientific reasoning appeals to evidence, consistency, understanding, and honesty.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The meaning and use of moral language must be distinguished from moral ontology: values are grounded in God's character and duties in divine commands, not in definitions of moral words.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Craig immediately before this first-person rebuttal, which explicitly restates his two contentions and addresses Harris by name.

components.text: Explain why the worst-misery evaluative anchor fails to provide an objective natural standard.
Answer the claim that natural facts governing minds and well-being are open to scientific investigation.

response.rationale: The semantics-versus-ontology distinction is issue-bearing and clarifies Craig's own account, but it does not answer the decisive natural-standard or inquiry warrants in the targeted earlier moves.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it contributes an important distinction but leaves the earlier naturalist inference substantially untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction among word meanings, ontological value grounds, and command-based duty grounds is explicit and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that semantics and ontology are distinct is well matched to the reasoning actually supplied.

charity.alternative: Harris may intend well-being as a substantive natural ground or criterion, not merely a definition of moral vocabulary.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even that stronger reading must still explain the ontological or normative relation between well-being and moral value.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction is internally coherent and cleanly separates semantic questions from Craig's two proposed ontological grounds.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Craig accurately restates his account, but the span mostly asserts rather than independently defends the divine grounding relations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary ontology-versus-semantics bridge rather than a central or motion-level completion condition.

representationalCharity.rationale: Craig states the semantic-ontological distinction accurately and preserves the legitimate grounding question, though he does not engage the strongest naturalist answer.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig distinguishes definitions of moral language from the claim that values are grounded in God and duties in commands reflecting divine nature.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Because good and evil persons could share well-being in a possible world, well-being and moral goodness are not identical and natural facts about flourishing alone cannot ground moral value.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig attributes the relevant admissions to Harris's book and develops the modal identity argument continuously in his rebuttal.

components.text: Show that the continuum of conscious well-being is identical with, or sufficient to ground, the full domain of moral goodness.
Show that scientifically investigable facts about flourishing exhaust the facts relevant to moral value.

response.rationale: Craig expressly argues that a possible divergence between well-being and moral goodness defeats identity and therefore blocks the inference from natural flourishing facts to moral value.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it explicitly identifies the identity premise, offers a modal counterexample, and states the grounding consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The modal argument is recoverable, but it sometimes shifts from rejecting identity to rejecting every grounding relation between well-being and goodness.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A genuine possible divergence defeats strict identity, but it does not by itself defeat supervenience, constitution, or a more limited criterion.

charity.alternative: Well-being may ground or track moral goodness without being strictly identical to every moral property across all possible worlds.
charity.decisiveQualification: A concession that the landscapes can diverge defeats identity but leaves weaker grounding relations available.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample coherently challenges identity, while the move leaves an unsupported bridge from nonidentity to total naturalistic incoherence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The reported modal concession supports the narrow result, but stronger grounding alternatives are neither documented nor seriously compared.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central objective-well-being bridge at its proposed connection between flourishing and moral goodness.

representationalCharity.rationale: Craig develops a serious modal objection but overextends it from strict nonidentity to the failure of all natural well-being foundations.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig invokes a possible-world divergence between the well-being continuum and moral landscape, then argues that strict identity and the proposed grounding fail.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Defining God as intrinsically good does not independently ground goodness, while beginning moral science from the badness of universal maximal misery is an axiomatic move comparable to those used in other sciences.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Harris, and the ensuing uninterrupted first-person response directly addresses Craig by name.

components.text: Explain why identifying God's nature as intrinsically good provides a nonarbitrary standard rather than a stipulative definition.
Show that theism supplies an independently warranted objective foundation unavailable to naturalism.
Apply the same objection to Harris's own axiomatic starting point without assuming the desired moral conclusion.

response.rationale: Harris directly challenges the nonarbitrariness of defining divine nature as good and offers universal misery as a comparable scientific axiom, though the evil-god possibility is only briefly developed.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive definitional-grounding demand and several related components but does not fully answer the modal necessity account.

precisionFindings.rationale: The alleged asymmetry and axiomatic comparison are clear, with an implicit distinction between a starting axiom and an independent derivation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The phrasing is appropriately limited as a challenge to Craig's supplied reason rather than a conclusive disproof of every divine-nature account.

charity.alternative: Craig can claim that goodness belongs essentially to the concept of a maximally great, worship-worthy God rather than being freely stipulated.
charity.decisiveQualification: That conceptual claim still needs to show that worship-worthiness noncircularly entails moral goodness and that such a being is possible.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The parity challenge is coherent, but the move does not fully show that Craig's conceptual entailment and Harris's misery axiom are structurally equivalent.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument supplies a clear conceptual comparison but limited defense of the evil-god possibility or the scientific status of its own axiom.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central nonarbitrary-divine-nature bridge and supports the supernatural critique.

representationalCharity.rationale: Harris presses the residual circularity fairly, although the brief evil-god comparison does not fully engage Craig's strongest modal-conceptual response.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris calls intrinsic divine goodness a definitional move, raises the possibility of evil gods, and contrasts it with his worst-misery starting point.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: God's essential goodness follows from the concept of a maximally great and worship-worthy being rather than from an arbitrary stipulative definition.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator begins the closing speeches, and Craig's first-person closing explicitly summarizes and defends his initial contention.

components.text: Explain why essential divine goodness follows from the concept of God rather than from arbitrary stipulation.
Address whether an evil god or several evil gods remain genuine conceptual alternatives.

response.rationale: Craig directly supplies a conceptual-entailment answer based on maximal greatness and worship-worthiness, but he does not independently exclude the evil-deity alternative or defend the relevant concepts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive arbitrariness component while leaving the rival-possibility component unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conceptual entailment is explicit, although the standards for maximal greatness and worship-worthiness remain implicitly moralized.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion follows only if maximal greatness and worship-worthiness include moral perfection, a premise not independently defended here.

charity.alternative: Harris's objection is that defining the greatest conceivable being through moral goodness may relocate rather than resolve the grounding question.
charity.decisiveQualification: Craig must show that worship-worthiness entails goodness without presupposing the evaluative standard under dispute.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The entailment is coherent under its conceptual premises, but the bachelor analogy obscures a material dispute over whether goodness is analytically included.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The span relies on conceptual assertion and analogy without a developed defense of maximal greatness, worship-worthiness, or possibility.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central divine-nature bridge by attempting to establish essential and nonarbitrary goodness.

representationalCharity.rationale: Craig answers the stipulation charge with a stronger conceptual account but does not fully meet the remaining circularity qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig argues that the greatest conceivable and worship-worthy being is essentially good, analogizing the entailment to unmarried bachelors.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Because materially similar apologetic reasoning supports incompatible religions, accidental birthplace and inherited doctrine make sectarian revelation an unreliable basis for moral knowledge and eternal consequences.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator assigns the closing to Harris, whose first-person argument contrasts Craig and Christianity with Islam.

components.text: Show that the conceptual argument for essential divine goodness fails or is equally available to an incompatible deity.
Distinguish the truth of a supernatural ontological foundation from reliable epistemic access through a particular revelation.
Address the explicit distinction between moral ontology and epistemic disagreement.

response.rationale: The competing-religion symmetry is significant contrary material about revelation reliability, but it does not contact the decisive ontological or conceptual premises of the cited pro moves.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it strongly bears on sectarian access while leaving the earlier supernatural-grounding inferences unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The epistemic symmetry claim is clear, but 'everything' and 'exactly the same' overgeneralize across potentially material doctrinal differences.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Comparable apologetic forms create a serious reliability challenge, but exact symmetry and unreliability require closer argument and comparison.

charity.alternative: Craig's ontological foundation may be independent of Christianity's revelation claims, and competing religions may offer materially different evidence.
charity.decisiveQualification: Similar inherited certainty and structurally parallel apologetics still undermine unargued reliance on sectarian access.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The birthplace and competing-claims considerations support epistemic caution, though the inference from similarity to equal evidential standing is underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Islam comparison is relevant but selective, with little representative evidence that the complete arguments and evidential bases are materially equivalent.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary bridge concerning the reliability of competing revelations and inherited traditions.

representationalCharity.rationale: Harris identifies a legitimate symmetry problem but materially compresses the ontology-access distinction and possible evidential differences.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris argues that substantially similar reasoning and scripture claims defend Islam, making birthplace and inherited sectarian commitment epistemically suspect.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Moral and spiritual truth should be pursued through present honest inquiry into the conditions of human flourishing rather than through competing sectarian claims about an invisible God.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage is the uninterrupted conclusion of Harris's closing and states his alternative to sectarian moral authority.

components.text: Answer the distinction between an objective moral foundation and fallible epistemic access to that foundation.
Explain why honest inquiry defeats the conceptual claim that a maximally great God is essentially good.
Explain how honest inquiry resolves the alleged modal divergence between well-being and moral goodness.

response.rationale: The appeal to honest inquiry offers a relevant epistemic alternative to sectarian revelation but does not answer the identified ontological or modal arguments in the earlier pro moves.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it advances a clear alternative method while leaving the decisive opposing premises uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The methodological proposal is clear, though 'the only tool we need' gives honest inquiry a broader and less specified scope than defended.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Honest inquiry is plainly important, but its exclusive sufficiency and the asserted lack of compelling supernatural evidence are not established here.

charity.alternative: A theist may regard revelation, philosophical argument, and shared inquiry as complementary rather than mutually exclusive methods.
charity.decisiveQualification: Competing unverifiable revelations still require public standards of assessment accessible to honest inquiry.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The preference for common inquiry over sectarian assertion is coherent, while the exclusivity conclusion does not follow without an argument excluding other evidence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The passage supplies a broad methodological assertion but little specific support for the absence of compelling evidence or inquiry's sole sufficiency.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary revelation-reliability bridge by proposing public inquiry as the epistemic alternative.

representationalCharity.rationale: Harris preserves the public-inquiry challenge but overstates the alternative as exclusive and does not engage a complementary-method account.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris contrasts Balkanized claims about an invisible God with present honest inquiry into the conditions under which human beings flourish.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Grounding morality solely in competent authority collapses the distinction between genuine harms and conventional rules, whereas moral understanding independently tracks effects on well-being.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris explicitly asks to add a point, identifies Craig's authority-based account, and develops his previously introduced psychopathy argument.

components.text: Explain why competent authority is insufficient to constitute moral duty when an authorized act still inflicts recognizable harm.
Address the qualification that divine commands are necessarily constrained by a holy and loving nature.
Show why an essentially good authority could nevertheless issue a genuinely harmful command.

response.rationale: The classroom comparison directly attacks authority as sufficient for morality, but ordinary teacher permission does not answer Craig's qualified appeal to uniquely competent and necessarily good divine authority.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the authority-sufficiency component but leaves the decisive divine-goodness qualification unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conventional-versus-moral distinction is clear, but the proposition broadens Craig's qualified divine account into morality grounded solely in generic authority.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The example defeats bare authority, but it does not by itself defeat authority constrained by an independently characterized necessarily good nature.

charity.alternative: Craig's account invokes divine authority uniquely constrained by essential holiness and love, not arbitrary permission from any competent official.
charity.decisiveQualification: If goodness must independently constrain authority, authority alone cannot explain the moral status of commands.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The example coherently distinguishes conventional permission from harm-based moral judgment, but its analogy to qualified divine authority is incomplete.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The child-judgment example is concrete and relevant, though it is anecdotal and does not establish the source or objectivity of the independent harm norm.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central divine-command bridge by challenging authority's sufficiency for objective duty.

representationalCharity.rationale: Harris exposes a real insufficiency in bare authority but materially weakens Craig's account by using an ordinary-authority analogue without its goodness constraint.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris contrasts permission to drink soda with permission to punch another child, arguing that people recognize harm as morally distinct from conventional rules.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: A deity that genuinely commanded sacrifice or comparable violence would thereby be evil, because the morality of the command can be judged independently of its purported divine source.
moves.attributionBasis: The statement is Harris's immediate first-person rejoinder to Craig's direct address and continues Harris's independent moral-evaluation argument.

components.text: Explain whether a purported divine command can be morally condemned independently of its asserted authoritative source.
Address the claim that the genuine greatest conceivable God is essentially good and therefore cannot issue an evil command.
Explain what natural or independent foundation gives the condemning judgment objective authority.

response.rationale: The rejoinder explicitly states that a genuinely violent divine command would make the commander evil, but it does not answer the impossibility qualification or ground the independent standard.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it directly contacts independent moral assessment while leaving two decisive grounding and necessity components unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: Despite its brevity, the conditional judgment is recoverable; the relevant kind and circumstances of sacrifice or violence remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The asserted condemnation is clear but unsupported in this short span and does not establish the independence or objectivity of its standard.

charity.alternative: Craig can deny the counterfactual antecedent because an essentially good God could not issue a genuinely evil command.
charity.decisiveQualification: That response still requires distinguishing impossible genuine commands from mistaken reports by an independently usable moral criterion.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional judgment is intelligible, but the conclusion largely restates the independent moral verdict rather than arguing for its standard or implications.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The extremely brief rejoinder supplies no evidence, warrant development, or comparison with the essential-goodness response.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central command bridge by asserting that source authority cannot convert an evil act into a moral duty.

representationalCharity.rationale: Harris forcefully states the independent-judgment intuition but does not engage the strongest essential-goodness qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris states that if God actually issued the violent command under discussion, that fact would make God evil rather than make the act moral.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Disagreement about applied morality concerns epistemic access rather than moral ontology, while objective values and duties require a transcendent ground beyond organisms, culture, and opinion.
moves.attributionBasis: The final audience question is expressly directed to Craig, and the answer restates his first-speech distinction and supernatural foundation argument.

components.text: Explain why disagreement and unreliable sectarian access do not by themselves defeat the existence or supernatural ground of objective moral facts.
Address whether shared honest inquiry is epistemically preferable to competing revelation claims.
Explain how applied moral judgment relates to the asserted divine ontological foundation.

response.rationale: Craig directly separates disagreement about perception and application from ontology, answering the inference from disagreement to nongrounding, but he does not answer the comparative reliability of inquiry and revelation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive ontology-versus-disagreement component while leaving the methodological reliability component unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The epistemic-ontological distinction is clear, but the added claim that atheistic humans are merely machines compresses several disputed implications.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Disagreement plainly does not entail nonexistence, but the further conclusion that objective value therefore requires transcendence is not established by that distinction.

charity.alternative: Harris's disagreement argument primarily challenges reliable sectarian access, not necessarily the bare existence of objective moral facts.
charity.decisiveQualification: Craig's ontology distinction defeats an ontological inference but leaves the revelation-reliability objection intact.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between what moral facts are and how people know or apply them is coherent, with the transcendence conclusion remaining underbridged.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinction is well supported, but the claims about atheistic agency and the necessity of a transcendent ground are largely asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary ontology-epistemology bridge rather than completing the supernatural motion route itself.

representationalCharity.rationale: Craig accurately states the distinction and its limited defeating consequence, though he underaddresses the strongest epistemic version of Harris's challenge.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig states that disagreements about perceiving and applying moral values are epistemological questions distinct from the ontological foundation he offers.
